models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods move as gifts that create obligations to return, a machine's gains could be shared through reciprocal duties, so those who gain from machines owe help to those whose work they replace. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that trust and status are built through exchange rather than price, obligations to share a machine's gains stay within known circles, so workers outside those circles who lose work have no claim on what the machine yields. Those with status in the group would decide when change comes. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that production serves the household's own needs, a family adopts a machine when it frees labour for those needs, so the gain stays in the household as less work for the same needs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a family farm balances its work against its needs rather than against profit, a household without capital for machines cannot share in their gains, and its members keep the heavy work by hand. The family alone sets the pace, so the poorest households may adopt last. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority collects goods as taxes and redistributes them, a machine paid from the common store could spread its gains across the whole population, and retraining could be funded from the same store. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre collects goods and decides their use, the authority alone would choose which machines to adopt and how fast, and the gains could flow to officials while workers whose labour the machines replace have no say in the change. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation; Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output is sold through trade, owners have a reason to adopt machines that raise output or take over the heaviest labour, which could lighten some toil, though the principle gives the enslaved no share of the gain. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through the ownership of people, a machine that makes some workers unnecessary would leave them with no education or property to move into, and the owners alone would decide whether they are kept, moved or sold. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe services to a lord in return for land and protection, a lord who adopts a labour-saving machine could ease those services, so the manor keeps its own supply and peasants keep their land. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe labour services and rents to a lord, a machine the lord owns could leave peasants paying for work it does, since the services and rents continue. The lord alone would decide when and how machines are used on the manor. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society; Capitulare de villis

models.best: Inferred from its principle that guilds regulate entry, training and quality, a guild could agree the terms for a new machine so that apprentices are still trained and the work keeps its standard, with the pace set inside the trade. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that statutes fix entry and training, a guild could keep out new machines and new entrants to protect its masters, so journeymen and the unskilled bear the cost of a slower or narrower change. The masters, not the workers, would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers; Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims at a trade surplus, the state could back machine industries that win export markets and use the surplus to fund training for the workers who move into them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production and trade for a surplus, machines could be restricted or steered to serve national trade, and colonial workers could bear the cost of change while merchants and the state set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade; Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, machines that raise farm output add to that product, and a single tax on land rent could capture part of the gain to fund the state without taxing the machines themselves. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that manufacture and trade create no net product, machines in workshops would count for little, so workers displaced from non-farm trades would have no claim to protection or to a share of the gain. Landowners and farmers, not those displaced, would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique; Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Robots and employment in Japan, 1978 to 2017 reports that falling robot prices raised robot installations and jobs across industries and commuting zones, which the authors read as machines and workers complementing each other. The summary was read, not the full paper, and a 2019 paper by the same team reports that the employment-to-population ratio fell where robot exposure was highest, so the sign is not settled.
models.worst: The worst practice here is answering machine-breaking with criminal penalties: Frame-breaking and the Frame Breaking Act of 1812 followed framework knitters' wrecking of frames at Arnold on 11 March 1811, and the Act covers stocking and lace frames. Sources disagree on the penalty, and several sites give February 1812 for passage while the statute text carries 20 March 1812. The statute was read only as an excerpt. Source: Statute of 1812 (52 Geo. 3 c. 16), text on a statutes website; Gedling page on the Luddites (undated in the results); a history piece and a Danish-hosted bibliography entry on the 1812 frame-breaking (both undated in the results)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, the prices of machines and labour show which machines are worth their cost, so firms adopt where the gain is real rather than tying up capital in the wrong ones. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion distorts production, cheap credit could fund a wave of machine purchases the economy cannot sustain. When credit tightens, idle machines and the workers who lose jobs with them bear the bust, while credit policy and state planning, not firms and workers, would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre; Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Bank tellers and ATMs in the United States reports that cheaper branches made more branches worth opening, though a blog adds that looser branching rules also fed growth, and the US teller workforce rose from about 250,000 in 1970 to around 500,000 by the mid-2010s. Teller work moved toward selling loans, credit cards and investments, and the figures come from summaries of the work, so precise numbers need care.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a smaller state with fewer controls leaves adjustment to markets, workers whose tasks machines take over may get little public retraining or income support, so the cost of a machine falls mainly on those who lose their work. Firms and private providers, not the public, would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom; Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism

models.best: Congressional hearings on automation, 1955 records a public study of jobs and investment: a joint House and Senate economic committee put automation on its study list, and its subcommittee held nine days of hearings that October on how automation might shape long-run jobs and investment. The hearing record was not read, and the results do not say what the hearings concluded or whether any law followed.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending is aimed at total demand and employment, a boom can create jobs overall while a district that loses a whole trade to machines stays out of work. The policy does not pick out which workers or places lose, so the cost of machines can fall on those least able to move. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory; Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services

models.best: West Coast longshore deal trading automation for benefits, 1960 reports that the longshore union accepted automation alongside a benefit package, and that its own division of the money gave 3 million a year to members' retirement, vesting and death benefits. It is one paper's account, the agreement text was not read, and the currency is not named.
models.worst: West Coast longshore deal trading automation for benefits, 1960 reports that work rules were traded for money: the union's own division paid 2 million a year for giving up some work rules. It is one paper's account, read as an excerpt, and the agreement text was not read; no currency is named, and the results cover only the West Coast. Source: Canadian lumber workers' paper, text in a digital archive (date not shown); deal terms also described in other search results that are not tied to this link

models.best: In Sweden's solidarity wage policy and job moves, one author's view, seen through an excerpt, is that a combined strategy kept solidarity pay from triggering mass layoffs in certain areas; the case concerns job moves, not machines. Inferred from its principle that active labour-market policy moves workers between jobs under national wage bargaining, a machine's displaced workers could be retrained and moved rather than laid off.
models.worst: In Sweden's solidarity wage policy and job moves, the article says some workers were uprooted geographically or made to switch trades, and that Swedish capital reaped the most benefit. It also asks whether the policy could have worked without large public-sector job creation. That is one author's view, seen through an excerpt, and concerns job moves, not machines. Inferred from its principle that active labour-market policy shifts workers, machine-displaced workers could be moved without consent, with national bargaining setting the pace. Source: Academic article in Spanish, 'Social democracy and capitalism: the neoclassical roots of the Swedish model' (English gloss of the title; year not shown in the results)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries and disciplines firms by performance, the state could steer machine investment into export industries, tie support to results, and move workers into the new trades. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks industries for credit and targets, workers in sectors left off the list, and firms that miss performance tests may be displaced by machines without help, while the state and its chosen firms set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle; Amsden, Asia's Next Giant

models.best: Inferred from its principle that land rent should fund public services, the gains from machines that raise land values would be taxed at source, so a land tax could pay for retraining without taxing the labour or capital that machines replace. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the tax falls on land and not on labour or capital, the gains from machines that raise output without raising land values would go untaxed, and displaced workers would have no claim on them. Landowners where machines are placed would collect the rent, and whoever holds the land would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities built by example replace wage competition, a community could adopt machines by agreement and share the time saved among its members, cutting hours for all rather than jobs for some. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities grow by example and planned association, a community that cannot raise capital for machines stays small, and workers outside it who lose work to machines have no shared gain to fall back on. Its planners, not the wider public, would decide who joins and when change comes. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society; Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit lets workers keep the full value of their work, workers who own their machines through mutual credit would keep the full gain from them, and each group of workers would set the pace of its own change. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that banks lend at cost and rent on property is abolished, a machine too large for one workshop could be out of reach if mutual credit is small, and workers who lose work to large firms would have no fund to fall back on. Each small producer would set its own pace, so change would be slow and uneven. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control their firms and share the surplus between users and workers, members can vote to adopt a machine and share its gain between lower prices for users and shorter hours or better pay for workers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that one member one vote gives control to current members, a firm may resist machines that threaten its members' jobs, while outside workers who lose work to rival firms have no say. Each firm's members would set the pace, so the gains could stay inside firms that already own machines. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes, the gain from a machine would reach everyone in the commune as shorter work or more goods, and no wage would be cut when work is replaced. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and that free association replaces contracts, no body can set one pace of change for all communes, so machines would spread unevenly, and communes without the machines or the willing members could fall behind with no common rule to help them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run industry through workers' organisations, the workers of each industry would decide whether and how fast to adopt machines, and could bargain for retraining and shorter hours before jobs are cut. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that unions run industry and may strike, a union could use strikes to halt machines in its trade, which protects its own members but leaves workers outside the union, and the unemployed, with no say and no share of the gain. A general strike could delay change across the whole economy. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT; Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: Inferred from its principle that socialism comes by democratic and gradual means, through public enterprise and a national minimum of welfare, a public enterprise could adopt machines while paying for retraining and a minimum income for those who lose work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that change comes gradually by democratic means, machines may be adopted slowly, and workers who lose their jobs in the meantime may wait for public enterprises and the welfare minimum to absorb them, with the pace set by elected majorities. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fabian Essays in Socialism; Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control through guild-like councils, the workers of each industry could negotiate the pace and terms of machines with consumers, and plan retraining before jobs are cut. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils of workers and consumers share control of an industry, a council of established workers may resist machines that would cut its own members' work, while workers outside it get no say. The state is only one partner, so councils that protect their own could set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and investment and the state mobilises labour for rapid industrialisation, the plan could adopt machines quickly across the economy and move workers into new industries at the same time. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state mobilises labour, workers could be moved to new work or new machines without their consent, and the gains and losses would be set by the plan rather than by the people affected, who would have no route to a share of the gain other than the plan. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System; First Five-Year Plan

models.best: Inferred from its principle that managers follow market prices within public ownership, a machine would be adopted where it lowers cost, and a central board could fund retraining and set rules that share the gain across the workforce. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, the board alone would decide whether machines are funded and whether displaced workers are retrained or left out, while managers adopt whatever cuts cost. The board, not the workers, would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism; Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that once classes disappear distribution follows need, machines that shorten necessary labour could free time for everyone, so the gain from machines would be shared by all rather than held by one class. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that distribution follows need only after the state withers away and classes disappear, the principle gives no rule for the transition, so the pace of machines and the sharing of their gains could be set by whoever holds the state while displaced workers wait for that end. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors runs alongside markets and special zones, firms in those zones could adopt machines where they pay and move workers into new trades, with gradual price reform under party direction setting the pace. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The worst practice here is robot use that, the study says, costs jobs and wages. Robots and jobs in China, as reported by a news site, says robot exposure significantly harms both employment and wages in a China Family Panel Studies analysis for 2010 to 2016. Only a headline and a short excerpt were read, so the methods and effect sizes cannot be checked; another panel finds falling jobs but no clear wage effect, so the wage finding is contested, and the case does not show who sets the pace. Source: The Register, a technology news outlet, reporting an academic study; reposted on a university website (year not shown)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, a machine would be adopted only after each council weighs its effect on jobs, and jobs would be balanced in complexity so that the dull tasks machines take are shared out. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils plan through repeated rounds of proposals, a change that machines bring could be slow to pass, and displaced workers would wait for the rounds to create new jobs. Neither markets nor central planners would set the pace, so the council process itself would decide it, and a council that stalls would delay everyone. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, machine adoption could be agreed trade by trade between employers and union bodies, with the state planning work for those displaced. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs industry toward national goals, including war, workers' organisations are state-controlled, so workers have no independent voice over machines, and displaced workers can be directed to other work for national ends. The state, not the workers, would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Italian corporative law; Nazi Four-Year Plan

models.best: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk, a machine could be financed by a partnership in which the financier shares the loss if it fails, and zakat could pass part of the gain to the poor. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited and finance shares profit and risk, workers paid from the profits of a machine financed by shared-profit contracts could lose pay if it fails, and displaced workers rely on zakat and family trust, which may not cover everyone who loses work. The partners in each contract would set the pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System; Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being and production is small-scale and local, machines that lighten drudgery in small workshops could be adopted where they serve people's well-being, keeping the gain close to the community. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production stays small, local and non-violent, machines that need large-scale output could be ruled out, so their gains go unused and the drudgery they could lift stays with those who do the work. Moderate consumption also limits demand for new goods, so change may come slowly and only where it fits small work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics; Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that property is spread widely and enterprises stay small, machines that small owners can afford would spread their gains across many households, and subsidiarity keeps decisions with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that small enterprise is the norm, small owners who cannot afford costly machines could be undercut by larger firms, and workers in firms that do adopt machines have no wider body to appeal to, since decisions stay with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum; Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that activity stays within planetary limits with no growth imperative, machines that cut resource use or shorten working time would be preferred, and the gain could be taken as time off rather than extra output. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, few new jobs may open in expanding sectors, so workers displaced in declining trades could find fewer openings, and the social floor must carry more of the cost. The planetary limits, rather than the workers, would set how fast machines spread. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics; Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, workers displaced by machines keep an income while they retrain or move, and everyone shares in machine gains through the land and resource taxes that fund the income. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is paid from taxes on land and natural resources, its level could fall short as machines take over more work, because the land and resource base need not grow with machine output. The pace of change would be left to markets, with the income as the only floor. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice; Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government that issues its own currency can fund full employment, the state could pay for retraining and a job guarantee for workers displaced by machines, with inflation watched as the limit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, a job guarantee could absorb displaced workers into low-productivity work, which slows the adoption of machines that would raise output. If spending runs ahead of what machines add to output, inflation rises, and the principle gives no guide to who should share the gains. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a community sharing a resource makes and enforces its own rules, the users of a shared machine could set its terms, share the time it saves, and monitor how it is used. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a community manages its resource with rules it designs, rules suited to a shared resource may not fit fast technological change or a wider economy, and outsiders who lose work to the same machines have no say in those rules. Each commons would set its own pace. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: Let machines be adopted where they pay, but pace each change by agreement between employers and workers, and share its gains: displaced workers get paid retraining and an income while they move, and no penalty may follow for resisting a machine. The pace is reviewed each year against outcomes for the workers displaced.
compromise.details: Keeps: price-led adoption that Robots and employment in Japan, 1978 to 2017 links to more jobs, though its sign is not settled (Classical laissez-faire capitalism); member votes to adopt a machine and share its gain (Cooperative economy). Blocks: penalties for resisting machines, as in Frame-breaking and the Frame Breaking Act of 1812, whose penalty is disputed (Classical laissez-faire capitalism), by a legal ban; displacement with no share of the gains (Gift economy), by a transition fund paid from machine profits. Test: displaced workers' re-employment at similar pay within two years, and employment in the most automated areas, measured yearly over at least ten years. Source: Adachi, Kawaguchi and Saito, 'Robots and Employment: Evidence from Japan, 1978-2017', RIETI discussion paper (2020); Statute of 1812 (52 Geo. 3 c. 16), text on a statutes website; Gedling page on the Luddites (undated in the results); a history piece and a Danish-hosted bibliography entry on the 1812 frame-breaking (both undated in the results); Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mauss, The Gift
